title: MagiCFirm: A Runtime for Magic-State Cultivation with Algorithm-Hardware Co-Design
authors: Jubo Xu, Abbas B. Ziad, Prakash Murali, Hongxiang Fan
abstract: Magic-state cultivation offers a promising alternative for lowering the cost of non-Clifford operations in fault-tolerant quantum computing (FTQC). However, realizing cultivation in practice exposes two challenges: (i) the lack of an open-source classical runtime layer between logical software and physical control, and (ii) the latency constraints on protocol-specific decisions that determine magic-state readiness. To address these challenges, we adopt an algorithm--hardware co-design approach. At the algorithm level, we develop a two-stage early-escape scheme that identifies an informative subset of detectors offline, constructs a compact decoding problem, and performs partial decoding in parallel with complete decoding at runtime, allowing high-confidence attempts to advance before full decoding completes. At the hardware level, we present MagiCFirm, a configurable runtime that combines offline-compiled microprograms with dedicated datapaths for detector construction, event processing, and protocol control, enabling end-to-end execution of magic-state cultivation. Across evaluated configurations, MagiCFirm reduces wall-clock magic-state preparation time by up to 39.3% at matched logical error rate. For a representative magic-state-bound workload, this translates to an estimated 11% reduction in overall application runtime.
summary: This paper introduces MagiCFirm, a novel hardware runtime designed to solve the latency and integration challenges in fault-tolerant quantum computing's magic-state cultivation process. By combining an advanced two-stage early-escape decoding algorithm with a configurable, event-driven hardware architecture, the authors significantly accelerate the preparation of magic states. This work moves the process from a theoretical abstraction to a concrete, high-performance, and resource-aware physical implementation.
main_problem: The practical realization of magic-state cultivation for fault-tolerant quantum computing (FTQC) is hindered by the lack of an open-source classical runtime layer and latency constraints on protocol-specific decisions.
main_result: The proposed runtime, MagiCFirm, reduces wall-clock magic-state preparation time by up to 39.3% and estimates an 11% reduction in overall application runtime for representative workloads.
method: The approach combines an algorithm-hardware co-design: developing a two-stage early-escape scheme for partial decoding and implementing MagiCFirm, a configurable runtime using offline-compiled microprograms and dedicated datapaths.
model_or_system: The system is based on FTQC using magic-state cultivation, which involves an Injection $ightarrow$ Cultivation $ightarrow$ Escape process. The physical implementation utilizes a fold-based measurement technique on a color-code layout.
key_observables: Wall-clock magic-state preparation time, overall application runtime, decoding confidence gap ($g_c(s)$), and Logical Error Rate (LER).
important_parameters: Logical error rate, detector firing outcomes, and the complementary-gap threshold ($t_c$).
main_assumptions: Existing high-level FTQC tools treat cultivation as a coarse-grained logical operation, leaving the online realization unspecified.
figures_summary: Figure 1 illustrates the magic-state cultivation workflow (Injection $ightarrow$ Cultivation $ightarrow$ Escape). Figure 2 details the detector-conditioned gap shift and latency breakdown. Figure 3 shows the MagiCFirm control-system architecture.
paper_structure: The paper addresses the challenges in magic-state cultivation by proposing a co-design. It details the algorithm-level early-escape scheme and presents MagiCFirm, a hardware runtime, which enables end-to-end, detector-driven execution.
why_interesting: While focused on quantum computing hardware, the emphasis on low-latency, resource-accountable, and event-driven classical control (the runtime layer) is highly relevant to any physical realization of quantum computation, including those using AMO platforms.

Figure 3. MagiCFirm control-system architecture. The left panels show offline compilation and hierarchical runtime deployment over an existing physical-control substrate, where PCore denotes the physical control core that directly controls the underlying qubits; the center panels detail the LCore and L2P architectures; and the right panel expands the configurable detector-construction datapath. Gray components denote the existing physical-control system, while colored blocks and black interconnects denote MagiCFirm extensions.

Figure 4. Partial mask geometric visualization. A rep- resentative time slice of the partial mask for 𝑑cultiv = 3, 𝑑escape = 15, 𝑝= 10−3, and 𝐾𝑄= 200. Red and gray cells denote retained and excluded detectors. (a) The LAP-selected base mask. (b) Structural closure augmented mask.
